shortQuestions: The main theme is the qualities that make a complete and successful man: self-control, patience, honesty, courage, balance in success and failure, perseverance and humility. Kipling advises his son that if he develops these virtues, the world will be his and he will be a true man.

Qualities in stanza two: to dream but not be ruled by dreams; to think but not make thoughts his only aim; to meet triumph and disaster calmly and treat both the same (as impostors); to bear his words being twisted by knaves; to see the things he gave his life to broken and rebuild them with worn-out tools.

It means that a man should be able to mix with great and powerful people without becoming proud, and still keep his simplicity and sympathy for ordinary people. Success and high company should not make him lose touch with the common man.

Triumph and Disaster are personified as two impostors: "If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster / And treat those two impostors just the same". The 'Will' that says "Hold on!" to the heart and nerves is also personified.

The title "If" is significant because the whole poem is a series of conditions: each 'if' states a quality a man must have. Only if all these conditions are fulfilled will the son become a true man — the title sums up this conditional advice.

"If you can fill the unforgiving minute with sixty seconds' worth of distance run" — time is precious and passes without mercy; we should use every second of every minute fully and productively, because lost time never comes back.

After listing all the qualities, the father says that if the son has them, the earth and everything in it will be his, and — what is even greater than that — he will become a true man: mature, complete and noble in character.
The rhyme scheme is ABAB (alternate rhyme) in each quatrain, e.g., 'you / you' and 'you / too' — giving four eight-line stanzas of the pattern ABAB CDCD.

Other qualities of a successful man: faith in Allah and honesty, hard work and discipline, good manners and respect for others, a thirst for knowledge, sense of responsibility, time management, kindness and helpfulness, leadership and the ability to work in a team.
activities: Sample essay — A Person with the Qualities of 'If': My grandfather is the person who reminds me of Kipling's poem. He remained calm in success and failure: when his business suffered a heavy loss, he did not complain but started again with patience. He never told lies and never hated those who wronged him. Though he met officers and important people, he never lost his common touch and treated the poor with kindness. He used every minute of his day well — prayer, work, reading and helping neighbours. These qualities made him a true man respected by all.

Role-play guide: 'fathers' advise 'sons' on behaviour in different situations — e.g., Son: "How should I behave if I fail an exam?" Father: "Do not lose heart; learn from mistakes and work harder." Son: "What if people blame me unfairly?" Father: "Stay patient and truthful; don't answer hatred with hatred." Students use the advice of the poem 'If' in their dialogue.
